text: Our life is what our thoughts make it. A man will find that as he alters his thoughts toward things and other people, things and other people will alter towards him.
suggested_reattribution: Composite: sentence 1 Marcus Aurelius (Meditations); sentence 2 James Allen (As a Man Thinketh, 1903)
notes: This is a splice of two different authors presented as one quotation. The first sentence, 'Our life is what our thoughts make it', is Marcus Aurelius, from the 'Meditations'. The second sentence is genuine James Allen, from 'As a Man Thinketh' (1903), where it reads 'A man will find that as he alters his thoughts towards things and other people, things and other people will alter towards him.' Attributing the combined text to Allen alone is wrong; the two halves should be separated or the Marcus Aurelius line dropped. | Suggested reattribution: Composite: sentence 1 Marcus Aurelius (Meditations); sentence 2 James Allen (As a Man Thinketh, 1903)

author: James Arthur Ray
text: There is no happiness if the things you believe are different than the things you do.
notes: This closely tracks a well-known line by the British travel writer Freya Stark, usually quoted as 'There can be no happiness if the things we believe in are different from the things we do', associated with her writing collected in 'The Journey's Echo'. The version here is a loose reworded form credited to the self-help author James Arthur Ray. I am confident the underlying thought is Stark's; recommend reattributing and restoring her wording, or dropping the quote. | Suggested reattribution: Freya Stark

author: Jeanne Kirkpatrick
text: We have war when at least one of the parties to a conflict wants something more than it wants peace.
suggested_reattribution: Jeane J. Kirkpatrick (spelling correction — same author)
notes: The author's name is misspelled in the corpus: the US diplomat and political scientist was Jeane J. Kirkpatrick (not Jeanne). The line is commonly credited to her and matches her realist idiom from the UN ambassadorship years, but I cannot place it in a specific speech, column, or book. Correct the spelling regardless of the provenance verdict. | Suggested reattribution: Jeane J. Kirkpatrick (spelling correction — same author)

author: John Christian Bovee
text: A failure establishes only this, that our determination to succeed was not strong enough.
notes: AUTHOR NAME ERROR: there is no 'John Christian Bovee'. The aphorist is Christian Nestell Bovee (1820-1904), American author, whose Intuitions and Summaries of Thought (1862) is the usual home for lines of this kind. The 'John' appears to be a corpus-level corruption. I am confident about the name correction; less so about the source volume, so I have not printed one. Recommend fixing the author field regardless of promotion. | Suggested reattribution: Christian Nestell Bovee

author: Anon.
text: A forest is a cathedral where the priest is nature.
notes: Credited to 'Anon.', and I can place no source at all. The line reads as a modern aphorism working a very old trope — the forest-as-cathedral figure runs from Bryant's 'The groves were God's first temples' (1825) through Muir and countless nature writers — but this specific sentence has no traceable origin I know of. Honest answer: unknown, probably an internet-era composition.

author: John Quincy Adams
text: If your actions inspire others to dream more, learn more, do more and become more, you are a leader.
notes: A known misattribution magnet. This is modern leadership-seminar prose — 'dream more, learn more, do more, become more' — and its diction is late-20th-century American management writing, not early-19th-century political English. Quote Investigator examined it and found no support in John Quincy Adams's writings, with the earliest sightings in the 1990s motivational literature. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I am not proposing a replacement author.

author: Jorge Luis Borges
text: The history of literature is not the history of authors and their careers, but the history of 'Spirit as the producer and consumer of literature.'
suggested_reattribution: Paul Valery (quoted by Jorge Luis Borges in "The Flower of Coleridge", Other Inquisitions, 1952)
notes: Borges did not say this — he quoted it. 'The Flower of Coleridge' opens by citing Paul Valery: around 1938 Valery wrote that the history of literature should not be the history of the authors and the accidents of their careers or of their works, but rather the history of the Spirit as producer or consumer of literature. The internal quotation marks in the corpus text are the tell that something is being relayed. Credit belongs to Valery, with Borges as the conduit. | Suggested reattribution: Paul Valery (quoted by Jorge Luis Borges in "The Flower of Coleridge", Other Inquisitions, 1952)

author: Joseph Campbell
text: We must be willing to let go of the life we have planned, so as to have the life that is waiting for us.
suggested_reattribution: E. M. Forster (per the Joseph Campbell Foundation's own correction; specific work unconfirmed)
notes: One of the most heavily misattributed lines in the Campbell corpus. The Joseph Campbell Foundation has publicly addressed it and points to E. M. Forster as the source; Campbell appears to have quoted or adapted it rather than coined it. A variant closer to Campbell's own phrasing ('We must let go of the life we have planned, so as to accept the one that is waiting for us') circulates from A Joseph Campbell Companion. I cannot name the Forster work from memory, so the reattribution below is offered as the documented candidate, not as a verified citation. | Suggested reattribution: E. M. Forster (per the Joseph Campbell Foundation's own correction; specific work unconfirmed)

author: Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim
text: Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible arise within us.
notes: This is the best-known line associated with the German Zen teacher and psychotherapist Karlfried Graf Durckheim (Graf Karlfried von Durckheim-Montmartin), and it matches his central theme of transformation through the 'exercise' of dying to the ego; it is usually cited from The Way of Transformation, though I cannot confirm that locus. The author field is garbled: 'Karlfried Gras Von Durkheim' should read 'Karlfried Graf Durckheim' ('Graf' is the German title Count, not a given name). Flagged as a name correction, not a change of author. | Suggested reattribution: Karlfried Graf Durckheim

author: Lakota proverb
text: When a man moves away from nature his heart becomes hard.
notes: Not an anonymous proverb. This is a lightly reworded line from Luther Standing Bear (Oglala Lakota), whose 'Land of the Spotted Eagle' (1933) contains the passage rendered as 'Man's heart, away from nature, becomes hard.' The 'Lakota proverb' label is the usual folk-anonymization of a named Native author, which strips him of credit. Confidence figure reflects the weak 'Lakota proverb' attribution; my confidence in the Standing Bear reattribution is considerably higher (~0.7), though the corpus wording is a paraphrase rather than his exact sentence. | Suggested reattribution: Luther Standing Bear

author: Lao Tzu
text: Time is a created thing. To say 'I don't have time,' is like saying, 'I don't want to.'
notes: Not in the Tao Te Ching. No chapter treats time as a 'created thing,' and the register — a self-help reframe about scheduling and willingness, complete with quoted colloquial speech ('I don't have time') — is unmistakably modern American. This circulates heavily in productivity writing as Lao Tzu, which is a textbook case of a modern maxim borrowing an ancient name for authority. I do not know who actually wrote it, so I offer no reattribution.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Give a man a fish and you feed him for the day. Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.
suggested_reattribution: Anne Isabella Ritchie (Mrs. Thackeray Ritchie), Mrs. Dymond, 1885
notes: Not Lao Tzu, and not a Chinese proverb. Nothing resembling it appears in the Tao Te Ching. The earliest known form traced by quotation researchers is in Anne Isabella Ritchie's novel 'Mrs. Dymond' (1885): 'if you give a man a fish he is hungry again in an hour; if you teach him to catch a fish you do him a good turn.' The saying has since been variously credited to Lao Tzu, Maimonides, and Confucius, all without support. Confidence value reflects the Lao Tzu attribution, which I regard as clearly wrong; my confidence in the Ritchie origin is high (~0.8). | Suggested reattribution: Anne Isabella Ritchie (Mrs. Thackeray Ritchie), Mrs. Dymond, 1885

author: Lao Tzu
text: Loving someone deeply gives you strength, while being deeply loved gives you courage.
notes: Not in the Tao Te Ching. This is one of the most heavily circulated pseudo-Lao Tzu lines on the internet, and the usual form is 'Being deeply loved by someone gives you strength, while loving someone deeply gives you courage' — note that the corpus version has the two clauses swapped, so it is a garbled variant of an already baseless attribution. Even the standard form has no identified author. Recommend removal or reattribution to 'Anonymous' if kept.

author: Leonardo Da Vinci
text: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.
notes: This is a well-known false attribution. The line does not appear anywhere in Leonardo's notebooks or the Trattato della Pittura, and the Italian version circulating online ('La semplicita e l'ultima sofisticazione') is a back-translation from English, which is itself strong evidence of modern origin. Wikiquote lists it under Leonardo's disputed/misattributed section. Its popularity comes largely from twentieth-century advertising use, notably the 1977 Apple II brochure, where it appeared as a tagline. I do not reliably know the true earliest coiner, so I am not naming one rather than guessing.

author: Leonardo Da Vinci
text: From an early age, I have abjured the use of meat, and the time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they look upon the murder of men.
suggested_reattribution: Dmitry Merezhkovsky (fictional dialogue in 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci', 1900)
notes: A documented case of fiction laundered into a quotation. The 'time will come when men will look upon the murder of animals as they now look upon the murder of men' line comes from Dmitry Merezhkovsky's historical novel 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci' (1900), where it is dialogue invented for the character of Leonardo. It appears in no surviving Leonardo manuscript. Leonardo's actual vegetarianism is separately evidenced — chiefly Andrea Corsali's 1515 letter to Giuliano de' Medici describing him as eating no meat — but that is not this sentence. Wikiquote files it as misattributed. | Suggested reattribution: Dmitry Merezhkovsky (fictional dialogue in 'The Romance of Leonardo da Vinci', 1900)

author: Louis Khan
text: Architecture is the thoughtful making of space.
suggested_reattribution: Louis I. Kahn (spelling correction, not a change of author)
notes: Genuine Kahn in substance, but two corrections are needed. First, the author's name is misspelled in the corpus: it is Louis I. Kahn (1901-1974), not 'Louis Khan'. Second, Kahn's formulation is plural — 'Architecture is the thoughtful making of spaces' — and it opens his contribution to Perspecta 4 (Yale architectural journal, 1957), continuing 'It is the creating of spaces that evoke a feeling of appropriate use.' I am confident of the sentence and of Kahn as its author; I am less certain of the exact issue and year, so I have left the print source null rather than risk a wrong citation. Fix the surname regardless of promotion outcome. | Suggested reattribution: Louis I. Kahn (spelling correction, not a change of author)

author: Lucille Ball
text: Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.
notes: This is James Baldwin, not Lucille Ball, and the misattribution is not close. The line comes from Baldwin's 1962 New York Times Book Review essay 'As Much Truth As One Can Bear', on the responsibilities of American writers; it is one of his most frequently quoted sentences and is well documented in Baldwin scholarship and collections. It has nothing to do with Ball, and the corpus has additionally filed it under 'humor', which compounds the error. Strong recommendation: reattribute to Baldwin or drop. | Suggested reattribution: James Baldwin

author: M.C. Escher
text: Only those who attempt the absurd will achieve the impossible.
notes: Circulates under Escher's name in design and business collections, but I know a closely matching line from Miguel de Unamuno — 'Solo el que ensaya lo absurdo es capaz de conquistar lo imposible' / 'Only he who attempts the absurd is capable of achieving the impossible' — which reads as the likelier origin. I cannot place the sentence in Escher's own writings (his essays and letters are fairly well documented and this is not a phrasing I associate with them). My Unamuno recall is solid on the Spanish wording but I cannot name the specific work, so the reattribution is offered as probable, not established, and the Escher attribution should not be promoted. | Suggested reattribution: Miguel de Unamuno (probable, not established)

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Keep my word positive. Words become my behaviors. Keep my behaviors positive. Behaviors become my habits. Keep my habits positive. Habits become my values. Keep my values positive. Values become my destiny.
notes: This is the 'thoughts become words, words become actions, habits become values, values become destiny' chain, one of the most durable false Gandhi attributions. No Gandhi source exists for it. Its ancestor is the 19th-century English maxim 'Sow a thought, reap an act; sow an act, reap a habit; sow a habit, reap a character; sow a character, reap a destiny', variously credited to Charles Reade and to Samuel Smiles and itself of contested origin; the modern positive-thinking chain is a 20th-century self-help reworking that later acquired Gandhi's name. I can identify the family the saying descends from but not a single true author, so I am leaving the reattribution null rather than guessing. Should not appear in the corpus under Gandhi.

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: There is no path to peace. Peace is the path.
notes: The documented origin of this formula is the American pacifist A. J. Muste, who said 'There is no way to peace; peace is the way' — a line strongly associated with him in the 1960s and quoted in coverage around his death in 1967. The corpus's 'no path to peace / peace is the path' is a variant of Muste's sentence, and the Gandhi credit appears to be later drift onto a bigger name, a pattern well documented for pacifist aphorisms. I am confident enough in the Muste attribution to name it, though I cannot cite the specific speech or article. | Suggested reattribution: A. J. Muste

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: Be the change you want to see in the world.
suggested_reattribution: Arleen Lorrance (probable origin of the wording); the underlying sentiment paraphrases Gandhi
notes: The single most famous thing Gandhi never said in these words. No source exists in his writings or speeches. The genuine passage it compresses is 'If we could change ourselves, the tendencies in the world would also change. As a man changes his own nature, so does the attitude of the world change towards him' — a different and more careful claim. The imperative-slogan wording appears to originate in 1970s American self-help; Arleen Lorrance's The Love Project material (c. 1974) carried 'Be the change you want to see happen', and the Gandhi credit attached later. Brian Morton's widely read 2011 New York Times piece 'Falser Words Were Never Spoken' laid this out. I name Lorrance as probable origin of the phrasing, but the sentiment is a fair paraphrase of Gandhi, so the corpus may prefer to carry the authentic longer passage instead. Do not promote under Gandhi as written. | Suggested reattribution: Arleen Lorrance (probable origin of the wording); the underlying sentiment paraphrases Gandhi

author: Mahatma Gandhi
text: An eye for an eye makes the whole world blind.
notes: The pre-flag is correct. No Gandhi source exists. The earliest credited appearances run through mid-20th-century secondary literature — Louis Fischer's The Life of Mahatma Gandhi (1950) carries a version of the thought as biographer's paraphrase rather than as a transcribed Gandhi sentence — and the line reached mass currency through Attenborough's Gandhi (1982), which drew on Fischer. The underlying reversal of lex talionis is older than Gandhi and circulated independently in English. Fischer is the likeliest proximate source of the wording, but as a paraphraser rather than an author, so I am recording that in notes rather than naming him as the quote's author.

author: Margaret Mead
text: We are continually faced with great opportunities which are brilliantly disguised as unsolvable problems.
notes: The well-documented form of this line belongs to John W. Gardner (Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare; founder of Common Cause): 'We are continually faced by great opportunities brilliantly disguised as insoluble problems,' associated with his mid-1960s writing and speeches. The saying has also drifted to Lee Iacocca and Charles Swindoll, and the Margaret Mead version appears in collections without any source in her published anthropological work. I know of no Mead text containing it. Confidence figure reflects the strength of the Mead attribution, which is weak. | Suggested reattribution: John W. Gardner

author: Marianne Williamson
text: Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.
suggested_reattribution: A Course in Miracles (Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976)
notes: This is not original to Marianne Williamson. It is, essentially verbatim, the third of the Fifty Miracle Principles that open the Text of A Course in Miracles: 'Miracles occur naturally as expressions of love. The real miracle is the love that inspires them. In this sense everything that comes from love is a miracle.' Williamson's 'A Return to Love' (1992) is a commentary on ACIM and quotes the Course extensively, which is how the line came to be tagged with her name. The attribution to her is a quoter-for-author error. | Suggested reattribution: A Course in Miracles (Foundation for Inner Peace, 1976)

author: Mark Twain
text: History doesn't repeat itself, but it does rhyme.
notes: The pre-flag is correct. No such line appears in Twain's published work, letters, or notebooks, and the attributions to him begin decades after his death in 1910 - the earliest instance I know of is a 1970 John Robert Colombo 'found poem' that presents 'History never repeats itself but it rhymes' as a Twain saying, which is a repetition of the claim rather than evidence for it. I cannot identify a true originator, so no reattribution is offered; classifying as apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed for exactly that reason. See also q_0975, a near-duplicate of this entry.

author: Mark Twain
text: Do the thing you fear most and the death of fear is certain.
notes: The pre-flag is correct: no source in Twain's published work or correspondence. The same sentence circulates just as often under Ralph Waldo Emerson's name, and that attribution is equally unsourced - Emerson's actual related line, from 'Heroism,' is 'Always do what you are afraid to do,' which he credits to his aunt Mary Moody Emerson. Because both major claimants fail and I cannot identify a real origin, apocryphal with no reattribution.

author: Mark Twain
text: Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things you didn't do than by the things you did. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Explore. Dream.
suggested_reattribution: Sarah Frances Brown, as recorded by her son H. Jackson Brown Jr. in P.S. I Love You (1990)
notes: The pre-flag matches what I know. Nothing in Twain's corpus contains this, and 'throw off the bowlines / sail away from the safe harbor' is not his register. The earliest documented appearance is in H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s 'P.S. I Love You' (1990), a collection of sayings from his mother, Sarah Frances Brown; the Twain tag attached afterwards and spread through 1990s self-help and graduation-speech material. Recording the true origin here because it is documented, not inferred - but note that Brown's book presents it as his mother's saying, so 'H. Jackson Brown Jr.' is the compiler rather than strictly the author. | Suggested reattribution: Sarah Frances Brown, as recorded by her son H. Jackson Brown Jr. in P.S. I Love You (1990)

author: Mark Twain
text: Worrying about something is like paying interest on a debt you don't even know if you owe.
notes: Not pre-flagged, but it should have been. No Twain source exists for this. It is a wordy variant of the unsourced 'Worrying is like paying a debt you don't owe,' which circulates under Twain, Will Rogers, and others without a citation for any of them. The one genuinely documented aphorism in this family belongs to William Ralph Inge, Dean of St Paul's: 'Worry is interest paid on trouble before it falls due.' The recorded wording differs enough that I will not reattribute it to Inge, but his line is the likely ancestor of the metaphor. Recommend flagging this entry as suspect.

author: Mark Twain
text: History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes.
notes: Same verdict as q_0970, of which this is a near-duplicate differing only by the word 'does' - the corpus is carrying both variants and should deduplicate. No Twain source; attributions post-date his 1910 death by decades, with the earliest I know of being John Robert Colombo's 1970 found poem. No identifiable true author, hence apocryphal with no reattribution.

author: Mark Twain
text: Age is an issue of mind over matter. If you don't mind, it doesn't matter.
notes: Not found in Twain's works or letters; Twain attributions for this line are late and unsupported. The 'if you don't mind, it doesn't matter' pun on mind/matter circulated as a stock joke well before it was pinned to any famous name. It is most commonly credited to Satchel Paige ('Age is a question of mind over matter...'), but Paige popularized rather than originated it, so I am not asserting a replacement author.

author: Mark Twain
text: When I was a boy of 14, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be 21, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years.
notes: A classic spurious Twain. It appears in no Twain work; documented appearances postdate his 1910 death, and it is biographically impossible as autobiography - John Marshall Clemens died when Samuel Clemens was eleven, so there was no father to rediscover at twenty-one. Origin unknown; the joke circulated anonymously in periodicals before acquiring Twain's name.

author: Marquis de Vauvengras
text: There is nothing that fear does not make men believe.
suggested_reattribution: Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues (author name is misspelled in the record)
notes: The maxim is Vauvenargues': 'Il n'est rien que la peur ne fasse croire,' from his Reflexions et maximes (published 1746 with the Introduction a la connaissance de l'esprit humain). The author field is misspelled and mistitled - it should read 'Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues', not 'Marquis de Vauvengras'. I am confident of the author, less so of the exact maxim number, so I have not cited one. | Suggested reattribution: Luc de Clapiers, marquis de Vauvenargues (author name is misspelled in the record)

author: Michael Gerber
text: If you don't know where you are going, any path will get you there.
suggested_reattribution: Popular paraphrase of Lewis Carroll's Cheshire Cat passage, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865); not original to Michael Gerber
notes: Confidence reflects the strength of the Gerber attribution, which is weak. This is a floating proverb that long predates Michael Gerber; it is the popular paraphrase of the Cheshire Cat exchange in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865) — 'if you don't much care where you want to get to, then it doesn't matter which way you go' — and also circulates in Yogi Berra's form ('you'll end up someplace else'). Gerber may well have used it in E-Myth-era writing, but quoting is not coining. No original-author claim should be recorded for him. | Suggested reattribution: Popular paraphrase of Lewis Carroll's Cheshire Cat passage, Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (1865); not original to Michael Gerber

author: Milton
text: I love everything that flows.
notes: Confidence refers to the recorded attribution to 'Milton,' which appears to be a parsing error rather than a real claim about John Milton. The line is Henry Miller's, from the celebrated passage in Tropic of Cancer (1934): 'I love everything that flows...' — and Miller's own sentence contains the phrase 'said the great blind Milton of our times,' his epithet for James Joyce. Almost certainly the corpus captured the word 'Milton' out of that clause. Note this sits adjacent to q_1040, also a Miller entry with a truncated author field, which supports the parsing-error reading. | Suggested reattribution: Henry Miller

author: Mohammed
text: Whoever knows himself knows God.
suggested_reattribution: Sufi maxim of uncertain origin, sometimes ascribed to Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi; not a canonical hadith
notes: This is the famous Sufi maxim 'man arafa nafsahu faqad arafa rabbahu' — 'he who knows himself knows his Lord' — widely quoted in Sufi literature (Ibn Arabi among many others) and often presented as a hadith. Classical hadith scholars rejected it: it appears in none of the canonical collections, and al-Nawawi, Ibn Taymiyya and al-Zarkashi among others judged it not established as a saying of the Prophet. It is sometimes ascribed instead to the early Sufi Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi. Attributing it flatly to Muhammad is not defensible. | Suggested reattribution: Sufi maxim of uncertain origin, sometimes ascribed to Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi; not a canonical hadith

author: Mohandas Gandhi
text: Never use violence of any kind. Never threaten violence in any way. Never even think violent thoughts. Never argue because it attacks another’s opinion. Never criticize because it attacks another’s ego. And your success is guaranteed.
notes: Almost certainly not Gandhi. The register is late-20th-century American self-help — the escalating 'never / never / never' construction and especially the closing promise 'and your success is guaranteed' are wholly foreign to Gandhi, who framed ahimsa as a discipline and a truth-practice, not as a technique with a guaranteed payoff. I know of no passage resembling this in the Collected Works or in his letters and speeches. Gandhi is one of the strongest misattribution magnets in the corpus, and this has the hallmarks of a seminar handout attributed to him for authority. No true origin identifiable, so no reattribution offered.

author: Mother Teresa
text: People are often unreasonable, illogical, and self centered; Forgive them anyway. If you are kind, people may accuse you of selfish, ulterior motives; Be kind anyway. If you are successful, you will win some false friends and some true enemies; Succeed anyway. If you are honest and frank, people may cheat you; Be honest and frank anyway. What you spend years building, someone could destroy overnight; Build anyway. If you find serenity and happiness, they may be jealous; Be happy anyway. The good you do today, people will often forget tomorrow; Do good anyway. Give the world the best you have, and it may never be enough; Give the world the best you've got anyway. You see, in the final analysis, it is between you and God; It was never between you and them anyway.
notes: This is one of the best-documented misattributions in circulation. The text is an adapted version of 'The Paradoxical Commandments,' written by Kent M. Keith in 1968 while he was a Harvard undergraduate, published in his booklet The Silent Revolution: Dynamic Leadership in the Student Council. A shortened version titled 'Anyway' was posted on the wall of Mother Teresa's children's home in Calcutta, which is how her name became attached; it was later reprinted in books about her, cementing the error. The closing 'it is between you and God' line is part of that Calcutta adaptation. Keith's authorship is well established and he has written about it publicly. | Suggested reattribution: Kent M. Keith

author: Mother Theresa
text: We can not do great things, just small things with great Love.
notes: One of the most durable and consistently attributed Mother Teresa lines; standard wording is 'We can do no great things, only small things with great love.' Attribution is uniform across decades of sources and she is recorded using the formulation in talks. The corpus entry has two hygiene problems: the author is misspelled 'Mother Theresa,' and the text is a garbled variant ('We can not do great things, just small things...') with inconsistent capitalization of 'Love.' I could not place the exact primary utterance, so this stays at strong-secondary rather than verified. | Suggested reattribution: Mother Teresa (author-name spelling correction only)

author: Mu Mon-kwan
text: It is so clear it is very hard to see. You must know that the fire which you are seeking is the fire in your own lantern, and that your rice has been cooked from the very beginning.
suggested_reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate / Mumonkan, c. 1228 — as a paraphrase, not a quotation
notes: 'Mu Mon-kwan' is not a person — it is a garbling of Mumonkan (無門關), the Japanese title of The Gateless Gate, the 1228 koan collection compiled by the Chinese Chan master Wumen Huikai (Japanese: Mumon Ekai). The underlying saying is Wumen's verse commentary, familiar in English from Paul Reps' Zen Flesh, Zen Bones as roughly: 'It is too clear and so it is hard to see. A dunce once searched for fire with a lighted lantern. Had he known what fire was, he could have cooked his rice much sooner.' The text here is a loose modern paraphrase, not any translation I recognize, so I am not citing the Mumonkan as the print source for this wording. The idea is authentically Wumen's; the sentence is not. | Suggested reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate / Mumonkan, c. 1228 — as a paraphrase, not a quotation

author: Muhammad Ali
text: Impossible is just a word thrown around by small men who find it easier to live in the world they've been given than to explore the power they have to change it. Impossible is not a fact. It's an opinion. Impossible is potential. Impossible is temporary. Impossible is nothing.
notes: This is advertising copy, not Ali. The passage is the manifesto text of the adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign launched in 2004, developed by the agency 180/TBWA, whose flagship spots featured Muhammad Ali (and archival footage of him alongside his daughter Laila). The final line 'Impossible is nothing' is the campaign tagline, which is the strongest tell. Ali's name and image were licensed to the campaign; the words were written for it. Widely recirculated as an Ali quotation ever since, including in books and on quote sites. I am confident the campaign is the origin and correspondingly low-confidence in the Ali attribution. | Suggested reattribution: adidas 'Impossible Is Nothing' campaign copy (agency 180/TBWA), 2004

author: Nagarjuna
text: Contentment is true wealth.
suggested_reattribution: Dhammapada 204 (attributed to the Buddha); Nagarjuna restates it in the Suhṛllekha, quoting the Buddha
notes: The canonical form of this saying is Buddhist scripture, not Nagarjuna: Dhammapada 204, 'santuṭṭhī paramaṃ dhanaṃ' — 'contentment is the greatest wealth.' Nagarjuna does echo it in the Suhṛllekha (Letter to a Friend), where he cites the Buddha to the effect that contentment is the supreme form of wealth, so the ascription is not baseless — but it makes Nagarjuna a transmitter rather than the author, and this four-word English form matches the Dhammapada rendering, not a specific Suhṛllekha translation I can name. Attribution as it stands is weak. | Suggested reattribution: Dhammapada 204 (attributed to the Buddha); Nagarjuna restates it in the Suhṛllekha, quoting the Buddha

author: Navajo saying
text: Bless those who challenge us to grow, to stretch, to move beyond the knowable, to come back home to our elemental and essential nature. Bless those who challenge us for they remind us of doors we have closed and doors we have yet to open. They are big medicine teachers for us.
notes: No credible traditional source. 'Navajo saying' is a generic ascription of exactly the kind that inspirational literature invents, and the language here is modern therapeutic English — 'challenge us to grow,' 'move beyond the knowable,' 'elemental and essential nature' — not translated Diné oral tradition. 'Big medicine teachers' reads as a settler-inflected pastiche of Native idiom. Pseudo-Native-American attributions are a well-documented category of fabrication (cf. the Chief Seattle speech). I know of no Navajo prayer, ceremonial text, or ethnographic record containing this. Recommend rejecting or relabeling as anonymous modern.

author: Oliver Wendell Holmes, Jr.
text: One's mind, once stretched by a new idea, never regains its original dimensions.
notes: Two errors compounded. The original is by Oliver Wendell Holmes SENIOR, the physician-essayist, not his son the Supreme Court justice: 'Every now and then a man's mind is stretched by a new idea or sensation, and never shrinks back to its former dimensions.' The familiar 'One's mind, once stretched by a new idea, never regains its original dimensions' is a 20th-century compression of that sentence, not Holmes's wording. Father/son confusion is the standard failure mode with this quote. Recommend reattributing to Holmes Sr. and, if the corpus wants exactness, restoring the 1858 wording. | Suggested reattribution: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.

author: Oscar Wilde
text: Be yourself; everone else is already taken.
notes: A well-known false Wilde. It appears nowhere in his works and the Wilde attribution is a late-20th-century development; earlier circulation of the sentiment is anonymous aphorism/greeting-card material. Classic misattribution-magnet behaviour. No credible author is identifiable, so apocryphal rather than likely_misattributed. (Input also misspells 'everone'.)

author: P. T. Barnum
text: No one ever made a difference by being like everyone else.
suggested_reattribution: The Greatest Showman (2017 film) — dialogue written for the P. T. Barnum character
notes: This is dialogue written for the fictionalised Barnum in the 2017 film The Greatest Showman, not a saying of the historical showman. The phrasing is modern-motivational and unlike 19th-century Barnum's prose. A large wave of pseudo-Barnum quotes entered circulation after that film. Reattribution is to the film's screenwriters; I am confident about the film origin but will not name individual credits from memory. | Suggested reattribution: The Greatest Showman (2017 film) — dialogue written for the P. T. Barnum character

author: Pablo Picasso
text: Good artists copy. Great artists steal.
notes: No evidence Picasso ever said this. The attribution was massively amplified by Steve Jobs quoting it in the 1990s/2000s. The documented antecedents belong to the literary-criticism tradition: W. H. Davenport Adams (1892) on poets who 'imitate and improve' versus those who 'steal and spoil', and T. S. Eliot in The Sacred Wood (1920), 'Immature poets imitate; mature poets steal.' Those are ancestors, not the same sentence, so I am not naming a single true author.

author: Patanjali
text: When you are inspired by some great purpose, some extraordinary project, all your thoughts break their bonds. Your mind transcends limitations. Your consciousness expands in every direction. And you find yourself in a new, great and wonderful world. Dormant forces, faculties and talents become alive and you discover yourself to be a greater person by far than you ever dreamed yourself to be.
notes: This passage does not appear in the Yoga Sutras in any translation I know. The Sutras are terse aphorisms in Sanskrit; this is expansive 20th-century motivational English ('dormant forces, faculties and talents'). It spread widely through Western business-creativity and New Thought literature in the 1980s-90s while carrying a 'Patanjali' label. Not Patanjali; I cannot identify the actual modern author, so no reattribution is offered.

author: Pema Chödrön
text: Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible in us be found.
notes: This is Pema Chödrön quoting someone else. The line originates with Karlfried Graf Dürckheim, the German psychotherapist and Zen teacher — his formulation runs roughly 'Only to the extent that a man exposes himself over and over again to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in him.' Chödrön quotes it (with attribution to Dürckheim) in her own work, most likely 'When Things Fall Apart', which is how it got detached and re-credited to her. I am confident about Dürckheim as the source author; I cannot name the specific Dürckheim title from memory. | Suggested reattribution: Karlfried Graf Dürckheim

author: Philip Toshido
text: We are, all of us, the divine spirit gazing upon itself in a gigantic mirror.
notes: I can find no author named 'Philip Toshido' in my training knowledge — not as a writer, teacher, or public figure — and the name itself looks irregular (Toshido is not a standard surname; this may be a corrupted or invented name). The sentiment is a generic Advaita/perennialist formulation that appears in many unattributed forms. Absence from my knowledge is not proof the person does not exist, but there is no credible attribution to record here and no basis for a reattribution.

author: Plato
text: Music gives a soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and life to everthing.
notes: A well-documented pseudo-Plato. This sentence does not appear anywhere in the Platonic corpus and has no Greek original; it is routinely listed among misattributed Plato quotations. Plato does discuss music's effect on the soul (Republic III, Timaeus), which is presumably how the line got attached to him, but the wording is modern and its actual author is unknown to me, so I am not offering a reattribution. Note this is a near-duplicate of q_1149, and this copy additionally contains a typo ('everthing').

author: Plato
text: Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.
suggested_reattribution: Ian Maclaren (pen name of Rev. John Watson)
notes: Not Plato. This is one of the best-known false Plato attributions; it appears in the misattributed section of Plato's Wikiquote page and has been traced by Quote Investigator to Ian Maclaren, the pen name of the Scottish author and clergyman John Watson, in the late 1890s, in the form 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.' The modernized 'Be kind... everyone you meet' wording is a later drift. The quote has also been falsely credited to Philo of Alexandria and to J.M. Barrie. Recording the reattribution to Maclaren with high confidence. | Suggested reattribution: Ian Maclaren (pen name of Rev. John Watson)

author: Plato
text: Music gives a soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination and life to everything.
notes: Same pseudo-Plato as q_1144, in its cleaner and more commonly circulated form. No such passage exists in Plato's works and there is no Greek original; it is a standard entry in lists of misattributed Plato quotations. Origin of the English sentence is unknown to me, so no reattribution is offered. Flagging as a duplicate of q_1144 for deduplication.

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: I slept and dreamt that life was joy. I awoke and saw that life was service. I acted and behold, service was joy.
suggested_reattribution: Derived from Ellen Sturgis Hooper's 1840 poem ('I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty'); the joy/service wording has no known author
notes: This is a known misattribution. The joy/service triplet is a 20th-century reworking of Ellen Sturgis Hooper's short poem published in The Dial (1840): 'I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty; / I woke, and found that life was Duty.' The 'service was joy' variant has been floated under Tagore, Gandhi, and Kahlil Gibran in different collections — a spread that is itself diagnostic — and I know of no passage in Tagore's works containing it. Quote Investigator has treated this family of variants and traced it back to Hooper. | Suggested reattribution: Derived from Ellen Sturgis Hooper's 1840 poem ('I slept, and dreamed that life was Beauty'); the joy/service wording has no known author

author: Rabindranath Tagore
text: I have become my own version of an optimist. If I can't make it through one door, I'll go through another door - or I'll make a door. Something terrific will come no matter how dark the present.
notes: Almost certainly not Tagore. The diction is modern colloquial American English ('my own version of an optimist', 'something terrific'), incompatible with Tagore's register in either Bengali or his own English renderings. I recognize this as a Joan Rivers line, widely quoted from her later interviews and her writing on resilience; the Tagore label appears to be a quote-site scrambling. I am confident it is not Tagore and reasonably confident it is Rivers, though I cannot name the specific book or interview. | Suggested reattribution: Joan Rivers

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To laugh often and much; to win the respect of intelligent people and the affection of children; to earn the appreciation of honest critics and endure the betrayal of false friends; to appreciate beauty; to find the best in others; to leave the world a bit better, whether by a healthy child, a garden patch, or a redeemed social condition; to know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.
suggested_reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), in an evolved and expanded form by later hands
notes: The 'What is Success?' passage — one of the most thoroughly documented Emerson misattributions. It originates with Bessie Anderson Stanley, whose prize-winning 1904 contest entry read 'He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'. The version here is a mid-20th-century expansion (the 'healthy child, a garden patch, a redeemed social condition' clauses are later accretions) that acquired Emerson's name in anthologies and greeting cards. It appears in no edition of Emerson's works. Emerson scholars and Quote Investigator both reject the attribution. | Suggested reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), in an evolved and expanded form by later hands

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.
suggested_reattribution: Probably a compressed rewording of e. e. cummings, 'A Poet's Advice to Students' (1955)
notes: Not found in Emerson's published works, journals, or letters as far as I know; the Emerson attribution is a 20th-century label with no textual support. The thought and structure track e. e. cummings closely: 'To be nobody-but-yourself in a world which is doing its best, night and day, to make you everybody else means to fight the hardest battle which any human being can fight' (A Poet's Advice to Students, 1955). The circulating 'Emerson' sentence looks like a compressed rewording of cummings. Emerson is a misattribution magnet for self-reliance aphorisms precisely because 'Self-Reliance' makes the sentiment sound like his. | Suggested reattribution: Probably a compressed rewording of e. e. cummings, 'A Poet's Advice to Students' (1955)

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: To laugh often and much; to win the respect of intelligent people and affection of children; to earn the appreciation of honest critics and endure the betrayal of false friends; to appreciate beauty, to find the best in others; to leave the world a bit better, whether by a healthy child, a garden patch or a redeemed social condition; to know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.
suggested_reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), heavily reworded by an unknown later hand
notes: This is the well-documented 'Success' poem misattribution. Emerson never wrote it; it appears in the Misattributed section of his Wikiquote page and has been traced by Quote Investigator to a 1904 prize-winning contest entry by Bessie Anderson Stanley ('He has achieved success who has lived well, laughed often, and loved much...'). The 'To laugh often and much / to win the respect of intelligent people' wording is a much later 20th-century rewrite of Stanley's text, circulated anonymously before being pinned on Emerson. I am confident it is not Emerson; I am less confident about who produced this specific rewrite. | Suggested reattribution: Bessie Anderson Stanley (1904), heavily reworded by an unknown later hand

author: Ram Das
text: All spiritual disciplines are done with a view to still the mind. The perfectly still mind is universal spirit.
notes: This does not read as Ram Dass; it reads as Advaita source material. I recall this wording — 'All spiritual practices are done with a view to still the mind. The perfectly still mind is universal spirit' — from Nisargadatta Maharaj's I Am That, the Maurice Frydman translation. My confidence in the reattribution is moderate (roughly 0.6), not high, and it could alternatively trace to Ramana Maharshi's recorded talks, which share this idiom. Either way the Ram Dass attribution looks incorrect. | Suggested reattribution: Nisargadatta Maharaj (probable; I Am That)

author: Rama Choomarasawmy
text: No distinction can be drawn between art and contemplation. The artists is first of all required to remove himself from human to celestial levels of appreciation; at this level and in a state of unification, no longer having in view anything external to himself, he sees and realizes, that is to say becomes, what he is afterwards to represent…
notes: 'Rama Choomarasawmy' is not a real person — it is a phonetic corruption of Ananda K. Coomaraswamy (1877-1947), the Ceylonese-British metaphysician and art historian. The passage is characteristic Coomaraswamy, from his writing on traditional art and the artist's identification with the form contemplated; my recollection points toward The Transformation of Nature in Art (1934) or Christian and Oriental Philosophy of Art (1943), but I cannot fix the book, so no print source is recorded. Confidence in the author correction is high (~0.85); confidence in the recorded name as given is near zero. Note also 'The artists is' in the corpus text is a typo for 'The artist is'. | Suggested reattribution: Ananda K. Coomaraswamy

author: Reverend Cecil Williams
text: "You've got to pray like it's all up to God, and work like it's all up to you."
suggested_reattribution: Traditional Christian aphorism, commonly attributed to Ignatius of Loyola
notes: Cecil Williams of Glide Memorial in San Francisco may well have said this from the pulpit, but he did not originate it. The aphorism is centuries older and circulates in two mirrored forms: 'Pray as though everything depended on God, work as though everything depended on you,' commonly credited to Ignatius of Loyola and also to Augustine of Hippo. Scholarship on the Ignatian version (Joseph de Guibert and others) notes the two halves get swapped between retellings, which is itself evidence of a long oral history. Treat this as a traditional Christian saying quoted by Williams, not authored by him. | Suggested reattribution: Traditional Christian aphorism, commonly attributed to Ignatius of Loyola

author: Saint Augustine
text: The key to immortality is first living a life worth remembering.
suggested_reattribution: Widely circulated as Bruce Lee (that attribution is itself unverified); not Augustine
notes: This does not read as Augustine in any register — not the Confessions, not the City of God, not the sermons — and 'a life worth remembering' as a route to 'immortality' inverts Augustine's actual theology, where immortality is God's gift and earthly fame is explicitly disparaged. The line circulates far more commonly attributed to Bruce Lee, in the sayings collected from his notebooks and popularized posthumously; that attribution is itself unverified, so I am flagging the Augustine attribution as wrong without asserting Lee as confirmed. | Suggested reattribution: Widely circulated as Bruce Lee (that attribution is itself unverified); not Augustine

author: Sir Winston Churchill
text: A lie gets halfway around the world before the truth has a chance to get its pants on.
suggested_reattribution: Jonathan Swift (1710, earliest documented form); the 'boots' variant is commonly credited to C. H. Spurgeon in the 19th century
notes: The Churchill attribution is spurious. This is a modern variant of a saying with a long documented pedigree: Jonathan Swift wrote 'Falsehood flies, and the Truth comes limping after it' in The Examiner (1710), and the 'boots' form — 'A lie will go round the world while truth is pulling its boots on' — circulated in the 19th century, commonly credited to the preacher C. H. Spurgeon, who himself presented it as an old saying. 'Pants on' is a 20th-century Americanized rewrite. Versions of this line are also misattributed to Mark Twain, another magnet. There is no evidence Churchill originated it. | Suggested reattribution: Jonathan Swift (1710, earliest documented form); the 'boots' variant is commonly credited to C. H. Spurgeon in the 19th century

author: Soren Kierkegaard
text: Be with what is, so that what is to be may become.
notes: I know of nothing in Kierkegaard's authorship resembling this, in any standard translation. The diction is modern therapeutic/mindfulness aphorism — the Gestalt 'paradoxical theory of change' register — not Kierkegaard's, whose treatment of becoming is far more elaborated and anguished. It reads like a coaching-literature line that acquired a prestigious name. I cannot identify the real originator, so I am not proposing a reattribution, but I would not promote this under Kierkegaard's name.

author: St. Francis de Sales
text: Never confuse your mistakes with your value as a human being. You're a perfectly valuable, creative, worthwhile person simply because you exist. And no amount of triumphs or tribulations can ever change that. Unconditional self acceptance is the core of a peaceful mind.
notes: Anachronistic. 'Unconditional self acceptance' is a term of art from Albert Ellis's Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, and the whole passage — separating mistakes from intrinsic worth, 'a peaceful mind' — is 20th-century cognitive-therapy and self-esteem language with no counterpart in the devotional writing of a 17th-century bishop. Francis de Sales wrote about gentleness toward one's own faults, which is probably why his name attached itself here, but his framing is theological (worth grounded in God), not psychological. I cannot identify who actually wrote this, so I am proposing no reattribution; Ellis is the likely conceptual source rather than a confirmed author.

author: St. Francis of Assisi
text: Start by doing what is necessary, then do what is possible, and suddenly you are doing the impossible.
notes: No evidence connects this to Francis of Assisi. It does not appear in his authenticated writings or in the early Franciscan biographies, and the earliest instances I am aware of are 20th-century, in motivational and recovery literature, where it circulated for some time before Francis's name was attached. The rhetorical shape — necessary, possible, impossible — is a modern three-beat inspirational construction. Widely repeated, which is not evidence.

author: Sydney Smiles
text: The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at a time.
suggested_reattribution: Richard Cecil, as quoted by Samuel Smiles in Self-Help (1859)
notes: 'Sydney Smiles' is not a person; this is a corruption of Samuel Smiles, the Scottish author of Self-Help (1859). In Self-Help, Smiles quotes the maxim from the Rev. Richard Cecil, whose usual wording is 'The shortest way to do many things is to do only one thing at once' — so even under the corrected name Smiles is the transmitter, not the author. My recollection of the Self-Help citation is good but not page-level; the confidence figure reflects the weakness of the attribution as recorded, not of the reattribution. | Suggested reattribution: Richard Cecil, as quoted by Samuel Smiles in Self-Help (1859)

author: T. S. Eliot
text: Time you enjoyed wasting is not wasted time.
notes: A well-documented misattribution. Eliot never wrote this; it appears in Marthe Troly-Curtin's novel Phrynette Married (1912) as 'Time you enjoy wasting is not wasted time', and Quote Investigator traced it there. Wikiquote lists it in the misattributed section of the Eliot page. Low confidence here reflects the near-certainty that the recorded attribution to Eliot is wrong. | Suggested reattribution: Marthe Troly-Curtin

author: Dalai Lama
text: Remember that not getting what you want is sometimes a wonderful stroke of luck.
notes: This is an item from the chain-circulated list 'Instructions for Life in the New Millennium', which spread by email in the late 1990s under the Dalai Lama's name. The Office of the Dalai Lama has disclaimed the list; it is not his, and several of its items track secular American self-help writing (H. Jackson Brown Jr.'s Life's Little Instruction Book is often noted as a source of similar material). Wikiquote treats the list as misattributed. I cannot identify the actual author of this specific line, so I offer no reattribution. A classic misattribution magnet — treat any bare 'Dalai Lama' aphorism in this register with suspicion.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: When you reach the end of your rope, tie a knot in it and hang on.
notes: The Jefferson attribution is almost certainly wrong. To my knowledge this line appears on the Jefferson Monticello foundation's list of spurious quotations — it is not found anywhere in his correspondence or published writings, and the idiom is twentieth-century American rather than eighteenth-century. It is also commonly credited to Franklin D. Roosevelt, which is itself unverified. Best current understanding is an anonymous early-twentieth-century saying that later collected famous names; because I cannot name the real originator with confidence, I am leaving the reattribution field null rather than guessing FDR.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: I'm a great believer in luck and I find the harder I work, the more I have of it.
notes: Not Jefferson. This is a documented spurious Jefferson quotation — it does not appear in his writings, and the Monticello foundation lists it among quotes wrongly ascribed to him. My recollection of Quote Investigator's research is that the earliest located version belongs to Coleman Cox, an American aphorist writing in the early 1920s, in the form 'I am a great believer in Luck. The harder I work, the more of it I seem to have'; the saying was later also pinned on Stephen Leacock and Samuel Goldwyn. I am naming Cox as the probable originator on the strength of that research but deliberately leaving earliest_print_source null, since I cannot confirm the exact volume and year without looking it up. | Suggested reattribution: Coleman Cox

author: Ts'ai Ken T'an
text: Water which is too pure has no fish.
suggested_reattribution: Classical Chinese proverb (Han-era; cf. Dongfang Shuo in the Book of Han) — not original to the Caigentan
notes: 'Ts'ai Ken T'an' is not an author — it is the Wade-Giles title of the Caigentan (Vegetable Root Discourse), a late-Ming aphorism collection by Hong Zicheng (Hong Yingming), c. 1590. The saying itself is considerably older than that collection: the Chinese proverb 'shui zhi qing ze wu yu, ren zhi cha ze wu tu' (water too clear has no fish; a person too exacting has no companions) is recorded in Han-dynasty sources, notably Dongfang Shuo's 'Answering a Guest's Objections' as preserved in the Book of Han, and in the Da Dai Liji. So the line is a classical Chinese proverb that the Caigentan may transmit rather than originate. The author field should at minimum be corrected to name Hong Zicheng or be marked as a Chinese proverb. | Suggested reattribution: Classical Chinese proverb (Han-era; cf. Dongfang Shuo in the Book of Han) — not original to the Caigentan

author: Unknown
text: I can complain because rosebushes have thorns, or I can rejoice because thorn bushes have roses.
suggested_reattribution: Paraphrase of Alphonse Karr, Voyage autour de mon jardin (1845); NOT Lincoln
notes: This is an English paraphrase of a genuine and much older line by the French writer Alphonse Karr, from Voyage autour de mon jardin (A Tour Round My Garden, 1845): some people grumble that roses have thorns; he is grateful that thorns have roses. The 'I can complain / I can rejoice' rewording is a later inspirational reformulation of unknown authorship, and it is also spuriously attributed to Abraham Lincoln — a classic Lincoln magnet attribution with no basis in his writings. Correctly listed as Unknown for this wording; the underlying thought is Karr's. | Suggested reattribution: Paraphrase of Alphonse Karr, Voyage autour de mon jardin (1845); NOT Lincoln

author: Unknown
text: If you don’t see God in all, then you don’t see God at all.
notes: Very widely circulated in Kundalini Yoga / 3HO circles as a saying of Yogi Bhajan (Harbhajan Singh Khalsa), where it appears in lecture transcripts and teaching collections. The attribution is consistent across that community but I cannot cite a specific dated lecture or printed volume, so it stays unverified. The sentiment also echoes older Sikh and Vedantic formulations, which makes an even earlier antecedent plausible. | Suggested reattribution: Yogi Bhajan (commonly credited; unconfirmed)

author: Unknown
text: Sometimes naked, sometimes mad, now as a scholar, now as a fool, thus they appear on earth - the free ones!
notes: This reads as an English rendering of a classical Sanskrit verse on the avadhuta / jivanmukta, and it is most often credited to Bhartrihari's Vairagya Shataka; it circulated in English-speaking spiritual circles partly through Ram Dass's use of it. I am reasonably but not firmly confident of the Bhartrihari source and cannot name the verse number or the translator, so the corpus author 'Unknown' is not wrong, merely incomplete. | Suggested reattribution: Bhartrihari, Vairagya Shataka (traditional Sanskrit; unconfirmed)

author: Unknown
text: Reach high, for stars lie hidden in your soul. Dream deep, for every dream precedes the goal.
notes: Consistently credited to Pamela Vaull Starr across greeting-card and anthology sources; the attribution is stable and specific enough to be worth recording, but I know of no primary publication, date, or verified biography confirming it. Stays below the promotion bar for that reason. | Suggested reattribution: Pamela Vaull Starr (commonly credited; unconfirmed)

author: Ursula LeGuin
text: The creative adult is the child who has survived.
notes: This is a well-documented misattribution. Le Guin herself denied writing it, stating on her own website that the line was not hers and asking that it stop being credited to her; quote researchers traced the sentence to the mathematics educator Julian F. Fleron, who wrote a close version in his own work before it drifted onto Le Guin. Confidence 0.15 rates the (weak) attribution to Le Guin, not the misattribution finding, which I hold with reasonable strength. Recommend removing Le Guin as author. | Suggested reattribution: Julian F. Fleron

author: Ursula LeGuin
text: The greatest religious problem today is how to be both a mystic and a militant; in other words how to combine the search for an expansion of inner awareness with effective social action, and how to feel one's true identity in both.
notes: Almost certainly not Ursula K. Le Guin. The vocabulary is that of academic religious studies — 'the greatest religious problem today', 'expansion of inner awareness', mysticism paired with social action — and Le Guin, a lifelong non-believer who wrote about Taoism in a very different register, is an implausible author. The likeliest explanation is a first-name collision with another Ursula in a quote list; the attribution I associate with this line is Ursula King, the scholar of mysticism and Teilhard de Chardin, whose subject matter matches exactly. I am not confident enough in that to enter it as a reattribution, so the field is left null. Recommend removing the Le Guin attribution regardless.

author: Vernon Saunders
text: Experience is a hard teacher, because she gives the test first, the lesson afterwards.
notes: The author name in the corpus is garbled. This is Vernon Sanders Law, the Pittsburgh Pirates pitcher and 1960 Cy Young winner — 'Vernon Saunders' appears to be his middle name mistaken for a surname. The saying is credited to him in a 1960 magazine piece and the attribution has been examined and upheld by quote researchers. Confident in the person; the exact publication date is from memory and should be checked before it is printed as fact. | Suggested reattribution: Vernon Sanders Law

author: Vincent van Gogh
text: Your profession is not what brings home your weekly paycheck, your profession is what you're put here on earth to do, with such passion and such intensity that it becomes spiritual in calling.
notes: Not van Gogh. The vocabulary is anachronistic and un-translatable back into his idiom: 'weekly paycheck' and 'spiritual in calling' belong to modern American self-help prose, not to the 1870s-80s Dutch/French letters to Theo. I cannot recall this passage anywhere in the collected letters, which are exhaustively indexed. It reads like a 20th-century vocation-and-calling passage that acquired a van Gogh byline. I cannot identify the real author, so no reattribution.

author: Wayne Gretsky
text: You miss 100% of the shots you don't take.
notes: Genuinely Gretzky's; he used the line in press interviews in the early 1980s and it spread from there. I do not have a reliable memory of the exact first newspaper column and date, so I have left the print source blank rather than guess. NOTE: the author field is misspelled 'Wayne Gretsky' — it should be 'Wayne Gretzky'. | Suggested reattribution: Wayne Gretzky (spelling correction only)

author: Wayne W. Dyer
text: It's never too late to have a happy childhood.
suggested_reattribution: Tom Robbins (probable; Still Life with Woodpecker, 1980 — unconfirmed)
notes: I recall this line as Tom Robbins's, appearing in his novel Still Life with Woodpecker (1980), and it also circulates as a recovery-movement slogan from roughly the same era. The Wayne Dyer attribution appears to be a later quote-site accretion — Dyer used the sentiment in talks, but he is not the source. I am confident enough about the Robbins origin to flag the Dyer attribution as doubtful, but not confident enough to call the reattribution settled. | Suggested reattribution: Tom Robbins (probable; Still Life with Woodpecker, 1980 — unconfirmed)

author: Will Rogers
text: If you find yourself in a hole, the first thing to do is stop digging.
notes: This is the proverbial 'first law of holes', which was in circulation as an anonymous saying well before it began being credited to Will Rogers, and it was later popularized in British politics by Denis Healey. Rogers attributions to it appear to be retrofitted. Probable true origin is anonymous proverb rather than a named author, so I have left suggested_reattribution null.

author: William Gilmore Simms
text: There is a peaceful quality to an authentic experience of love that penetrates to our core, touching a part of ourselves that has always been there. True love activates this inner being, filling us with warmth and light. An authentic experience of love does not ask us to look a certain way, drive a certain car, or have a certain job. It takes us as we are, no changes required. When people truly love us, their love for us awakens our love for ourselves. They remind us that what we seek outside of ourselves is a mirror image of the lover within. In this way, true love never makes us feel needy or lacking or anxious. Instead, true love empowers us with its implicit message that we are, always have been, and always will be, made of love.
notes: Almost certainly not William Gilmore Simms, who died in 1870. This passage is unmistakably modern therapeutic self-help prose — 'authentic experience of love', 'activates this inner being', 'the lover within', plus the anachronistic 'drive a certain car'. An automobile reference alone rules out a nineteenth-century author. The style closely matches contemporary daily-inspiration writing of the DailyOM sort, but I will not name an author I cannot confirm. Recommend rejecting the Simms attribution outright; this looks like a quote-site database collision, possibly compounded by the adjacent genuine Simms entry (q_1451).

author: William James
text: The greatest weapon against stress is our ability to choose one thought over another.
notes: Strongly doubtful as William James. 'Stress' in the psychological sense used here is a mid-twentieth-century coinage — Hans Selye's work from the 1930s onward — and would have been anachronistic for James, who died in 1910; he wrote about strain, worry, and habit, not 'stress'. The sentence also has the compressed, modern self-help cadence of a wellness-poster line rather than James's prose. I know of no source in his writings. Recommend dropping the James attribution; true origin unknown.

author: William Shakespeare
text: We cannot conceive of matter being formed of nothing, since things require a seed to start from... Therefore there is not anything which returns to nothing, but all things return dissolved into their elements.
suggested_reattribution: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (probable; classical Epicurean source — not Shakespeare)
notes: Not Shakespeare — nothing in this diction, doctrine, or vocabulary belongs to him. This is classical Epicurean physics: nothing comes from nothing, things arise from 'seeds', and nothing perishes into nothing but dissolves back into its elements. That is the argument of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura, Book I, and 'seed' renders the Lucretian semina. Pliny the Elder states a close version in the Natural History, so I cannot be certain which classical author this English translation comes from, and I do not know the translator. Confident it is not Shakespeare; only probable that it is Lucretius. | Suggested reattribution: Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (probable; classical Epicurean source — not Shakespeare)

author: Winston Churchill
text: Success is not final. Failure is not fatal. It is the courage to continue that counts.
notes: A well-known Churchill fake. It does not appear in the Churchill canon, and the International Churchill Society lists it among quotations he never said. Quote Investigator traced early forms to 1930s American motivational and advertising copy ('Success is never final and failure never fatal; it's courage that counts'), well before it was pinned to Churchill. I recall that provenance but will not present it as a citation. No true author identifiable.

author: Winston Churchill
text: We make a living by what we get, but we make a life by what we give.
notes: Not Churchill. Absent from the Churchill canon and listed by the International Churchill Society among quotations wrongly credited to him. The saying circulated in the early twentieth century before being attached to his name; it is also attributed to Norman MacEwan, though I cannot confirm that claim, so I am not naming a replacement author.

author: Winston Churchill
text: If you're going through hell, keep going.
notes: One of the most confidently repeated Churchill quotations he demonstrably never said. It appears in no speech, book, letter, or contemporary record; the International Churchill Society lists it as misattributed, and researchers have found no instance before the late twentieth century, decades after his death. Origin unknown.

author: Yogi Berra
text: The future isn’t what it used to be.
suggested_reattribution: Paul Valery (earlier form, 1930s); popularized in English by Yogi Berra
notes: Berra used the line and claimed it in 'The Yogi Book: I Really Didn't Say Everything I Said!' (1998), so the attribution is not baseless — but the saying substantially predates him. It is commonly traced to Paul Valery, who wrote in the 1930s that the future 'is no longer what it used to be' (Regards sur le monde actuel), and English instances appear well before Berra's career-quote fame. Berra is the popularizer, not the originator. Confidence here reflects confidence in the attribution AS GIVEN, which is weak; my confidence in the earlier-origin finding is considerably higher. I have not confirmed a page/edition for the Valery line and so leave the print source null. | Suggested reattribution: Paul Valery (earlier form, 1930s); popularized in English by Yogi Berra

author: Yunmen Wenyan
text: If your mind isn’t clouded by unnecessary things, this is the best season of your life.
suggested_reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate, case 19 verse
notes: This is the second half of Wumen Huikai's verse to Case 19 of the Wumenguan ('Ordinary Mind is the Way'): 'Hundreds of flowers in spring, the moon in autumn, a cool breeze in summer, snow in winter. If your mind isn't clouded by unnecessary things, this is the best season of your life.' (若無閑事挂心頭，便是人間好時節). Not Yunmen Wenyan — the confusion likely arises because Yunmen is the source of the similar-sounding 'Every day is a good day' (Blue Cliff Record, case 6). I am confident in this reattribution. | Suggested reattribution: Wumen Huikai (Mumon Ekai), The Gateless Gate, case 19 verse

author: Zen proverb
text: Seek not to follow in the footsteps of the ancient masters. Seek what they sought.
notes: Not an anonymous proverb — this is Matsuo Basho, from the short prose piece commonly translated as 'Words by a Brushwood Gate' (Saimon no ji): 'Do not seek to follow in the footsteps of the men of old; seek what they sought.' The rendering in wide English circulation comes largely through Robert Aitken's 'A Zen Wave: Basho's Haiku and Zen' (1978); I recall the attribution firmly but not the exact page, so I leave the print source field null rather than guess an edition. | Suggested reattribution: Matsuo Basho (1644-1694)

author: Zen proverb
text: Do not seek the truth, only cease to cherish your opinions.
notes: This is a line from the Xinxin Ming (Hsin Hsin Ming, 'Verses on the Faith Mind') traditionally attributed to Jianzhi Sengcan, the Third Chan Patriarch (d. 606): 不用求真，唯須息見 — 'Do not seek the truth; only cease to cherish opinions.' Genuinely Zen, so the category label is not wrong, but a specific text and author are identifiable and should replace 'Zen proverb'. Traditional authorship of the Xinxin Ming is itself disputed by scholars (the text is likely later than Sengcan), which is why I do not go higher. | Suggested reattribution: Jianzhi Sengcan (traditional), Xinxin Ming

author: Zen proverb
text: To follow the path, look to the master, follow the master, walk with the master, see through the master, become the master.
notes: No basis in any Chan or Zen text I know. The five-step 'look to / follow / walk with / see through / become the master' progression is a modern Western self-development formulation of the kind that gets a 'Zen proverb' label attached to it on quote sites. Zen literature tends in the opposite direction on this theme (see Basho's 'seek what they sought', or Linji's 'if you meet the Buddha, kill him'). Recommend treating as unsourced modern coinage.

author: Zen proverb
text: All of the significant battles are waged within the self.
notes: This is an item from Sheldon Kopp's 'An Eschatological Laundry List: A Partial Register of the 927 (or was it 928?) Eternal Truths', the closing list of his 1972 book. The book's Zen-flavored title (from the Linji koan) is very likely why items from that list drifted into circulation as 'Zen proverbs'. I recall this specific item with reasonable confidence; I do not recall a page number and so do not give one. | Suggested reattribution: Sheldon B. Kopp

author: Zen proverb
text: You must become somebody before you can become nobody.
notes: This is Jack Engler's well-known formulation from his work on the interface of psychoanalytic developmental theory and Buddhist meditation: 'You have to be somebody before you can be nobody.' It first appeared in his 1984 Journal of Transpersonal Psychology essay on therapeutic aims in psychotherapy and meditation, reprinted in 'Transformations of Consciousness' (1986). Its Buddhist subject matter is why it gets relabeled a Zen proverb; it is a 20th-century academic coinage, not a traditional saying. I am confident about Engler and the essay, less so about exact bibliographic details. | Suggested reattribution: Jack Engler

author: Zen saying
text: Not always so.
notes: As a generic 'Zen saying' this is untraceable — it is a three-word English phrase, not a rendering of a known koan, sutra line, or classical Chan formula I can place. The reason it circulates in English is Shunryu Suzuki: 'Not always so' is remembered by his San Francisco Zen Center students as one of his habitual correctives, and it supplies the title of the posthumous collection 'Not Always So: Practicing the True Spirit of Zen' (Suzuki, edited by Edward Espe Brown, HarperCollins, 2002), drawn from lectures given in the late 1960s and early 1970s. I am confident that book and title exist; I cannot pin the phrase to a specific dated lecture or to any pre-Suzuki print occurrence, so I am not recording an earliest print source. Suggesting Suzuki as the proximate English source rather than an anonymous tradition, but flagging that he was himself gesturing at a general Zen attitude, so 'Zen saying' is loose rather than flatly wrong. | Suggested reattribution: Shunryu Suzuki

author: Zen saying
text: To know and not do is not yet to know.
suggested_reattribution: Wang Yangming (paraphrase; popularized in English via Stephen Covey)
notes: Not Zen. This is the signature doctrine of the Ming neo-Confucian Wang Yangming (1472-1529), the unity of knowing and acting (zhi xing he yi), stated in the Chuanxi lu / 'Instructions for Practical Living' roughly as: there have never been people who know and do not act; those who know but do not act simply do not yet know. The English wording here matches the paraphrase popularized in Western business and self-help writing — Stephen Covey used a near-identical line ('To know and not to do is really not to know') in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), which is likely how it entered circulation with a vague Eastern-wisdom label that later hardened into 'Zen saying'. I am confident about the Wang Yangming doctrine and reasonably confident about the Covey transmission path; I am not confident enough about which translation produced this exact English sentence to name an earliest print source, so I am leaving that null rather than guessing at a Wing-tsit Chan page. | Suggested reattribution: Wang Yangming (paraphrase; popularized in English via Stephen Covey)
